thread.title: Boeing Engineers and Tech Workers Approve Contract, Avoid Strike
thread.title_full: Boeing Engineers and Tech Workers Approve Contract, Avoid Strike

author: priyanka.patel tech editor
title: Boeing Engineers and Tech Workers Approve Contract, Avoid Strike
text:
Boeing engineers and technical workers approved a four-year contract on Thursday, securing immediate wage increases and averting a strike that threatened aircraft production schedules and federal regulatory approvals in Washington and other western states.
Contract Approval and Voting Margins Across SPEEA Units
Members of the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace approved a sweetened four-year contract on Thursday, concluding a high-stakes bargaining cycle that followed the rejection of an earlier proposal in August.
The union represents roughly 17,000 workers across Washington, Oregon, California, and Utah, with the majority of its membership located in the Puget Sound region. Voting concluded at noon on Thursday after about a week of electronic balloting.
The professional unit, which represents approximately 13,000 engineers and scientists, voted 67.62% in favor of the deal, with 7,895 members casting yes votes and 3,780 voting no. The technical unit, representing about 4,000 analysts, technicians, planners, and specialists, approved the agreement by a narrower margin of 53.48%, with 2,061 votes in favor and 1,793 opposed, on an 89% turnout.
This outcome contrasts sharply with the August vote, when 64% of the professional unit and nearly 72% of the technical unit rejected Boeing’s initial offer and authorized a strike.
Wage Increases and Salary Projections Over Four Years
The newly ratified contract delivers a pay boost over four years, up from the raise proposed in the rejected August offer.
Workers receive an immediate 10% ratification wage increase effective Friday, followed by annual raises of 4%, with an increase of up to 6% based on merit.
- Engineers (Professional Unit): Average base salary increases from $152,000 to $208,000 over the life of the contract.
- Technical Employees (Tech Unit): Average base salary increases from $119,000 to $163,000 over the contract term.
Workers also receive an extra day of paid leave to use before the end of the year.
Stakes for Airplane Certification and Production Schedules
Approval of the labor agreement averts a potential work stoppage that would have coincided with the expiration of the previous contract on October 6. Aviation analysts noted that a strike would have halted engineering development and regulatory compliance work at a critical juncture for the aerospace manufacturer.
“Let me be clear—we’re working very hard to try to avoid any kind of a work stoppage. That’s our key priority because the impact would be significant. Essentially, the 777-certification program shuts down until we get the engineers back, and it would have a ripple effect into our production.”
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg
Industry analysts observed that avoiding a strike protects the company’s path toward financial recovery following a costly two-month machinist strike in 2024.
“The stakes were really high. Certification of the new Boeing 777 and the MAX 10 kind of hung in the balance. Those programs surely would’ve been delayed if the engineers and technicians had gone on strike.”
Hardee added that concluding the negotiation process represents a positive development for Boeing as it attempts to stabilize monthly 737 MAX production and secure federal approvals, though the Federal Aviation Administration continues to evaluate software issues affecting landing procedures on the 737 MAX 10.
Workplace Provisions, Artificial Intelligence, and Remaining Union Priorities
Beyond compensation, the contract addresses working conditions, remote arrangements, and emerging workplace technologies.
The agreement enhances health care and retirement benefits, introduces two additional vacation days, a new floating holiday, and three bereavement days. Mandatory overtime limits are reduced from 144 hours to 96 hours a quarter for professionals and to 112 hours a quarter for technical workers.
To address concerns regarding the shifting of tasks to nonunion facilities, Boeing agreed to provide union representatives with workforce updates twice a year regarding specific job codes.
Despite securing these provisions, union representatives stressed that labor-management friction remains an ongoing concern.
Ben Nimmergut, Boeing’s vice president and functional chief engineer for Production Engineering, expressed satisfaction with the vote. We look forward to working with our team to support our company’s continued recovery and meeting our customer commitments now and into the future,
Nimmergut said in a statement.
